content: Cefaclor is a cephalosporin-type antibiotic used to treat a variety of bacterial infections, including those affecting the middle ear, skin, urinary tract, and respiratory tract. It is not effective against viral infections such as the common cold or flu. When using cefaclor, the oral suspension should be shaken well before each dose. It can be taken with or without food, as directed by your doctor, typically every 8 or 12 hours. To maximize its effectiveness, it is important to take the medication at evenly spaced intervals and to complete the full prescribed course, even if symptoms improve after a few days. Common side effects of cefaclor include stomach upset, headache, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. While these are generally mild, the medication may rarely cause a severe intestinal condition due to Clostridium difficile, which can occur during treatment or weeks to months after stopping the medication. Prolonged or repeated use of cefaclor may lead to oral thrush or a new vaginal yeast infection. Serious allergic reactions to cefaclor are rare but possible. Before taking cefaclor, inform your doctor if you are allergic to it, penicillins, or other cephalosporins, or if you have any other allergies. This product may contain inactive ingredients that could cause allergic reactions or other problems. Cefaclor may interfere with the effectiveness of live bacterial vaccines, such as the typhoid vaccine. During pregnancy, cefaclor should only be used when clearly needed, as its effects on nursing infants are unknown. Exercise caution when administering cefaclor to breastfeeding women. Drug interactions may alter how cefaclor or other medications work or increase the risk of serious side effects. For example, cefaclor can decrease the effectiveness of oral hormonal contraceptives by altering intestinal flora, though the risk of contraceptive failure is low. It may also increase the toxicity of aminoglycosides (e.g., gentamicin, tobramycin) by enhancing nephrotoxic and/or ototoxic effects. Additionally, cefaclor can interfere with the therapeutic effects of immune checkpoint inhibitors (e.g., nivolumab, pembrolizumab) and live bacterial vaccines. Always inform your doctor and pharmacist about all medications and supplements you are taking to avoid potential interactions. Cefaclor should be stored at room temperature (20-25°C or 68-77°F) in its original form. Reconstituted oral suspensions should be refrigerated and used within 14 days. Do not freeze the suspension. Discard any unused portion after 14 days. In case of an overdose, seek immediate medical attention. In the U.S., call 911 for severe symptoms such as loss of consciousness or difficulty breathing, or contact a poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. In Canada, call 1-844-764-7669. Cefaclor should only be prescribed for proven or strongly suspected bacterial infections to avoid the development of drug-resistant bacteria. Superinfections caused by the overgrowth of non-susceptible organisms should be considered during treatment with broad-spectrum antimicrobials, and appropriate measures should be taken if they occur. Patients with reduced kidney function may require dosage adjustments. For creatinine clearance of 10-30 mL/min, the dose should be reduced by half, and for clearance below 10 mL/min, the dose should be reduced by three-quarters. High doses may cause central nervous system toxicity. Cefaclor is generally considered safe during pregnancy when necessary, but there are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women. Animal reproduction studies are not always predictive of human response. The medication passes into breast milk, so caution is advised when administered to nursing mothers. This information is a summary and does not include all possible details about cefaclor. It is not a substitute for professional medical advice. Always consult your healthcare provider for complete information about this medication and your specific health needs.
